blocks.x: We're recording today at 2115 Toledano Street and this is Bob Michelle. Yeah.
Yeah.
Let's get your name on it.
Sonny William. S-O-N-N-Y. William.
And what's your, is that your name that you got? That's my name, yeah. You would name that one. That's not a nickname.
No.
I never heard anybody call you anything else. I wanted to ask you that. Yeah, I wanted to see something. We didn't put the date on here yet. What's today's date?
Today is the 13th.
So it's Friday the 13th of January? Yeah. 1961. Mm-hmm. Let's see. This is a contract here for Sonny Williams Jazz Band. Yeah. Music for all occasions from Uptown 7933.
That's an old telephone.
Mm-hmm. And it says 2031 Fuchsia Street. Fuchsia Street. Yeah. So let's see. What year would this be when you lived there on Fuchsia? Well, I just moved here three years ago.
So.
I lived there 36 years.
You lived 36 years on Fuchsia?
I'm Fuchsia Street, yeah.
Mm-hmm.
So you had this for quite a while? Yeah. How old is it you think these contracts are?
These contracts is now, I got those contracts in 1927. Hmm.
It says, New Orleans Louisiana 19, and then you fill in the year. Contract with, we the Sonny Williams Jazz Band.
Jazz Band.
Jazz Band. To hereby agree to furnish a band of blank pieces for a blank. And it goes on to this, for the sum of so many dollars. Mm-hmm. Received on account, so many dollars in the balance.
So much.
So much else. We play that blank and it has an M. Did they pay you before the job or after the job?
We pay so much on the job. Mm-hmm. But deposit on the job. A deposit and then.
A deposit and then.
Deposit and when the job is ended, it pays the balance. Let's see.

It says, it is further agreed that if any, if for any cause whatsoever, the body mentioned fails to comply with this contract, the deposit will be forfeit and relinquish all claims of the Sonny Williams Jazz Band. That's right. And then they have a place for the signature of the manager. Yeah. Who was the manager of the band?
Was that you?
Oh, the manager and all. The manager and leader of all. Yeah.
You know the, the manager, it's all up to the manager.
The fellow was playing, he don't have no word.

The manager would take these jobs, it's up to him, they're looking for him. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Says, Benabe. He was there. Benabe's the man who made the contract. Benabe Print Shop 2434 Louisiana Avenue. Was he a musician or anything? No, he wasn't no musician. He had an uncle who was a trombone player.
He used to play trombone with me. But he's dead now. What was his name?
His name was Usain Benabe. Usain Benabe. Yeah. Usain Benabe. Yeah.
Mm-hm. I've heard of the Benabe's. It seems to me they were related to the kellies someone.
He had an uncle who was a trombone player. He used to play trombone with me. But he's dead now.
What was his name?
His name was Usain Benabe.
Usain?
Yeah.
I've heard of the Benabe's. Seems to me they were related to the Kellys song.
He was Ernest Kelley's uncle.
Oh yeah. Yeah. Yeah, little dad I think told me about him.
Little who? Little dad, the band. Now listen, is dad living?
No, he's dead.
He's dead, eh?
He died a long time ago now.
Yeah.
Maybe close to a year.
I didn't see how dad could play. He couldn't hear good. But he played pretty good.
Well, I guess if somebody tuned the thing for him, he wouldn't have any trouble.
Mm-hmm.
You don't have any extra one of these, huh?
Yeah, you can take one of those.
Yeah, we'd like to keep that. I certainly appreciate that. Well, let's see. Maybe we better start back in the beginning of your life. When were you born?
I was born 1889.
Mm-hmm. The exact day?
Exact day. 26th of December.
Oh. You just had a birthday not too long ago. That's right. I bet you didn't get many presents.
I got a couple presents from my two daughters.
Well, I mean, you got Christmas presents and birthday presents at the same time.
Yeah, same time, yeah. They said I'm from Portland, Oregon. Mm-hmm.
You just... When you were a little boy, you must have kept your parents for Christmas and then they...
They used to keep me both. My oldest boy back then now. Yeah. They used to keep me both.
Now, I mean your mother and father.
Well, I don't know my father. My father died when I was quite young.
Mm-hmm.
My mother, she died in 41.
Did they play any music?
No. I don't think I played.
Who was that?
His name was Buddy Blair. Buddy Blair?
Yeah. Who did he play with?
I don't know. He was playing with a band out in Central Park. Where were you born, by the way? I was born in Le Comte.
Where?
Le Comte.
Oh, yeah.
It's a rapid parish. About 18 miles on this side of Alexander.
Mm-hmm.
This is born. I raised them in Central Park, though.
Oh, I see. Mm-hmm. How old were you when you went to St. Charles?
About six months old.
And where did you live in St. Charles?
At Emma.
Oh, that's... Who's that trombone player from there?
Well, we had Ernest Kelly from there. We had a father by the name of Val Eugene. He was a trumpet player. We had a couple trumpet players from there. They all did now.
Did you know Eddie Atkins?

That's my... That's the boy me and him. He started together. Mm-hmm. I was playing guitar. Yeah, I know him. We came up together. Went to school together. Well, they all did. Eddie died. Freddy died. And the other boy died. So they all did now. Freddy, which is Freddy? Freddy, that's Eddie's brother. Yeah.
That's the one.
That's the one. That's the one.
That's Eddie's brother.
That's Eddie's brother. Next door to Eddie. No, we didn't put our names on here.

Well, stop it for a minute. You want to put your name on here? Marjorie Zander. And how about putting your name on here since you're listening too? Houston. Mm-hmm. And you're his son? Older son. Mm-hmm.
And I'm Dick Allen. Mm-hmm.
Well, let's see. We were talking about Eddie Atkins and you were mentioning somebody. Eddie Atkins, that's my homeboy. Yeah. I'm Dick Allen. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .

Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . where we came from, where I used to play. Eddie, he started with us on trombone, playing a vowel trombone. Right to him up. Come here, he played there a while, left there, went Chicago. But he came right on back home, he died at home.
When did he come back home?

Well, near as I can guess about six years ago. It might be a little older, it might be about seven years. Came back home from Chicago. He went to the Army from Chicago. And I got a friend by the name of Dixon, told me that Eddie was the head trombone player in that military band from Chicago.
Did he start playing jazz or was he reading?
He was reading when he started. He started under Professor Alford. He was reading. He was a good reader.
What about, we better get some more about your uncle out there that played. He played alto horn or alto saxophone?
He played alto horn.
And what was the band that he played?
I done forgotten the name. All I could tell you is St. Charles Bass Band. There was a bass band at home right there, St. Charles Bass.
Do you remember any of the fellows in that band?
Oh yes, I heard the band play. But I never heard him play. He died. He didn't, he didn't, he wasn't in there so very long, he died. But the band, I heard the band play often.
Was it a reading brass band?
Oh yeah, sure, it was a reading brass band. Damn dumb for this, a man who teaches that brass band. Quite a grandfather. Well did he let them play some numbers by head
or would they do that or what? Oh no, they used to play music. Only reading music.
Yeah, they used to play music.
Do you remember the guys' names, any of them? Oh, I would tell you some of them, I forgot plenty of names.

Yeah, well the names. Well Arthur Griffin, he was a trumpet player. Arthur? Griffin. And as young you said trombone. Martin Rowland Tuvo. Ernest Bernabe Alto. Henry Bernabe Barrington. Caleb Hamilton Clarinet. I see who else, they had, what's his brother's name, played rhythm. Marshall Bennett, a snare rhythm player. I can't think about the bass rhythm player's name.
How big a band was it?
A band about 14 pieces. Yeah, I heard them play it regularly. They come up. They all was older than me. They all was playing.
That sounds like a, must have been something to hear out there.
Oh yeah, it was all that. Like during election, they played all over the past during election.
Mm-hmm. Did they ever have any competition? Any battle of bands or anything? No.
No. Not to my knowing. Never had any competition at all.
I thought maybe they'd get together with a band from up around Reserve or something.

No. They never did get in the Reserve Band. They were the one that was, they were right in the parish playing during the election time. They had the band, the Pickford Band from St. John, but they didn't ever come down alone and play. Mm-hmm.
What would happen during election time that they'd play for?

Well, there, this fellow running for different orchestras, they would hire them to play. They'd go from one place in the parish to the other place playing. That's the way they used to do it a long time ago.
Would they play when the man was making a speech or something? No, they'd play after they'd make a speech.

Oh, actually. They'd make a speech and they'd play. They'd play several tunes after they'd make a speech. Mm-hmm. You remember any of the tunes they played? No, I don't remember any. Must be a good one, but I can't wait. But when was that?
That'd been over 40 years ago. Over 40 years?
That's close to 52 years ago.
Mm-hmm. Was that band set up when you were a little boy? Oh, yeah. Set up when I was a little boy.

So it was going and organized and everything. Yeah. And then, you know, I was going to play every tune after they'd be a speech. Mm-hmm. You remember any of the tunes they played? No, I don't remember any of them. That's been a good one, but I can't wait. But when was that? Yeah. When was that?
That's been over 40 years ago. Over 40 years ago. That's close to 52 years ago. When was that band?
When you were a little boy? Oh, yeah. Set up when I was a little boy.
So it was going and organized and everything.
Yeah. It was set up when I was a little boy. I had another fellow by the name of Lewis Horace. He used to play trumpet too. Mm-hmm.
What about Joe Adrian? Did he ever play out that much?

Well, Joe Adrian used to come play home now and then. He used to play violin before we played trombone. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. You know Lewis was a man? I never met him. I just missed him. So I just missed him. Lewis was a really good music writer.
Good writer. Was he from Atlanta or from here? No, he's from here.
I know him from here. I know him from here. Oh, yeah. He was a really good music writer.
He was a really good music writer. Good writer.
Was he from Atlanta or from here? No, he's from here. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

home playing guitar. We had a seven piece band. Let's see. We had Caleb Hamilton on clarinet, Joseph Bennett on violin, Willie Lee on bass violin, and Ed Atkin on trombone, Usain and I were on trumpet. Who was the leader? Who was the leader? Caleb Hamilton was leading C clarinet. He would play the melody? Play the melody, the violin part with the C clarinet. So your trumpet part must have been different then? Well during that time, he used to use two clarinet, a B and an A. So he played a violin part with the C clarinet. Clarinet played well, he had a B and an A. And then like today, you'll figure that B, that C sharp and that A, you'll figure that out. From the music, but before, you had the instrument to play. What kind of part did the trumpet play?

What would he play? The trumpet play lead? He'd play lead, yeah. He'd play lead then. Trump would play lead, violin lead. So you had the two guys would be both playing lead, the clarinet and the clarinet.
Yeah, clarinet and the trumpet. See the C trumpet was playing the real clarinet, the violin part.
The C clarinet was playing the violin. Yeah. I see. Yeah. I see.
Mm-hmm. Funny.
Must have made music sound entirely different. Yes, it sounds all right. Mm-hmm.

Violin, when you get up in the high register with the C clarinet, it sounds now like a violin. Mm-hmm. But if you fall, blow the satin a little way, you see. When you get down on the G string on the violin, you make the clarinet sound like that.
Did the trumpet players play as fast as they do now? Faster or what?

No, about the same way. They was playing two-four times. The only time wasn't playing like this split time, like that two-four music you split it, you know? Mm-hmm. I mean four-four, you split it, make two-four. They played two-four, but they're not four-four. They played losses, shatters. Mm-hmm. They don't play that no more. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
What kind of part did the trombone play then?

Trombone part, he had the solo. The same as they do now? Yeah. No, they didn't lead at all on the trombone then. They only had the solo making all the time. Mm-hmm. But now most of them lead on the trombone. Mm-hmm. But during that time, you know that. Mm-hmm.
Well, when you were playing guitar, did you take lessons?
Yeah, I took lessons on guitar. Mm-hmm. But I tell you why I quit the guitar. I wanted to sing. I couldn't sing. I quit.
Mm-hmm. Did you take lessons from somebody in particular? From Professor Andre.

Oh, he taught guitar too? Yeah, he was a professor. He taught all the ministry. Mm-hmm. Well, how would he give you lessons? Would you be alone or would you be in a crowd? He'd give every man, he'd give so many minutes on a lesson. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
So he teach every man and he teach the band both?
Yeah.
I see. Get the band in there and rehearse them.

Yeah, after they get lined up on it, then he rehearses them. You see? Yeah. Old man is fine. But play a clarinet too. Now he teach trombone. I never heard him play trombone. He teach trombone. He plays the trumpet, clarinet, violin, bass violin.
Well I guess in those times if he could play trombone, he could play trombone. Wasn't that much different then?
They both was two kids.
And they had the vowel trombones there. Yeah.
They had the vowel trombones.
They'd be just about the same as playing a trumpet for a trombone.
Well, the trombones, they used the bass clip. The trumpet and the treble clip. That makes a difference.
Yeah, well I mean it would just be the same note but lower.
Yeah.
That's what I'm talking about. They both make a B-flat with all the valves up.
That's the way he makes a B-flat with a... With a trombone.
With a valve trombone it would be the same way.
With all the valves up.
Yeah, just... And if you want to make a C, you press down the first and third fingers.
That would be D on the trombone. Yeah, well...

That'd be D, you know? Well, I think it's the same note but they write a different tone, I don't know. Yeah. And concert pitch. I forget. But they're both... The finger just about the same way, you know? It's the same principle.
Well, I don't think they got so very many a vowel trombone players now.
Not many. I don't know anybody around town that plays it much now.
Well, the last man I know who played the bell trombone was a fella by the name of Willie Connish. That's the last man I know who played the bell trombone.
Did he ever change the slide? Oh yeah, he changed the slide.
He changed the slide.
Would it make much difference in their playing when they changed the slide? Did they make a different style of playing?
Well, they mix a whole lot of slower and it would slower better with the slide than with the band trombone. When did you start playing guitar?
Nineteen...eight.
Nineteen...eight. Nineteen...eight. Nineteen...eight.
So after two years, you changed then, huh?
I changed. I went on clarinet a while. I quit the clarinet in 1925. Got on trumpet.
Nineteen...five?
Quit the clarinet.
Was that a B flat or C or did you have to play them all then?
I had a C. C and a B.
Let me put that down for you, you tear it up. Oh, I've got plenty of them.
You've got plenty of them.
I was worried you were going to ruin it. I have plenty of them.
Tear that contract up.
Yeah. So, in those days, until you switched the trumpet, you were playing all of them, huh?

Yeah, I was playing all of them. All the different kind of clarinet. Yeah. No pitch, no high pitch clarinet. Mm-hmm. Albert system. When did the people here start using the Bane? Oh, pretty good wire. The clarinet ain't more easy than Albert system. I never did pull the Bane system.
When you quit clarinet, was there anybody playing Bane here in the town?
No, not to my remember to no.
Who did you play your first job with on clarinet?
Well, I was playing with the Bull Band. Playing big clarinet in the Bull Band.
What band is that?

They had a big club right out there. See where the Capitol Lodge meets that? They had a 14-piece brass band there. And I was playing clarinet in that band. Some way or another they couldn't keep no trumpet playing so I told the leader I'm going to take up trumpets. And I bought them at home. That was for the club? Yeah.
Where the Elks is now, that was the Bulls club. The Bulls club.
Were you a member of the Bulls? No, I never was no member.
I see. But they had men in their band who weren't members. Well, yeah, they had several of them in the band who were members of the club.
Who was in the band? I don't know a few of them, but I don't know a few of them. But I don't know a few of them.
Were the kind of guys that they had, were they playing in other bands too?
No, they were one that was playing in the bull bass band. Like that fellow played trombone by the name of . . . . what's his name? I didn't forgot the most of them.
Were the kind of guys that they had, were they playing in other bands too?

No, they were only playing in the bull bass band. Like that fella played trombone, and by the name of, what's his name? Anyway, I forgot his name. He played trombone. I was playing trumpet then. I tried to get him to come on the job and play it with me. He said, no, he don't play no obviously music. He played nothing but brass band music.
And did he ever change your order?
No, he still stayed on that trombone, the brass band. Steve, what is Steve's other name? I can't call his other name.
Is he still around today? No, he's gone.
He's gone.
I thought maybe I'd know him.
Yeah, he's gone. I was thinking last week, week before last, I said, the only fella I had in my band, every one of them, there he's gone.
You were in that band in the country for two years, you say? Yeah, that's out at my home.
I came down here in 1918.
Were you playing clarinet out in the country at all?
Yeah, I was playing clarinet, playing the C clarinet. But with who?
Just with yourself or with the band? I hadn't gotten a band yet.
I only played guitar in the band.
And so you came here in 1918, did you get a job right away playing clarinet? No, I didn't get a job right away.

I didn't get a job until a little bit before I got in the Bull Bass Band. I started playing with them 1920, I believe it was. Buckaloocy, went to Buckaloocy in 1921, played a Labor Day parade over in Buckaloocy. Was that with the Bull? Yeah, that was the Bull Band.
What was the job you had before the Bull Band?
The job I had?
Mm-hmm.
The job I had before that, I was playing on music, I was working.
Oh, I see. Mm-hmm. But I thought maybe you played one or two little jobs before you got with the Bulls, some music job.
I played several jobs, but not here.
Oh, I see. Mm-hmm. With who would they be with?
I played with different fellas out in the country. Mm-hmm.
Out around the name of them?
Yeah. A fella by the name of Val Eugene, he's a trumpet player. Mm-hmm. I played with him, put a good ball on him.
I wonder if he's related to these trombone players around town. What, they got Homer Eugene and Wendell Eugene, they're two brothers?
They'd be realistic to them. Where they from?

Well, they live downtown now. Yeah, below that Dutch canal. Well, I know on the other side of the canal somewhere, Canal Street, I can't remember where. Mm-hmm. So, how long did you stay with the Bulls band?
About four years. About four years. About four years. Five years.
Five years.
Mm-hmm.
And you changed to trumpet in 1925. And when you were playing with the Bulls brass band, did you do any officer work then? No, they didn't do no officer work. Mm-hmm.

He was doing officer work for the dance. Something I wanted to ask you about was who were some of the other bands that you heard when you were quite young, like out in the country, who did you hear that come out there from the city? Well, I heard the Olympia. Mm-hmm.

Eddie Atkins played with the Olympia when he came back home. Eddie Walk Cliff, he came home several times. Where was he from? Where was he from? He was from St. James but he had been down there. Mm-hmm . What are some of the other bands that you heard when you were quite young, like out in the country, who did you hear that come out there from the city?
Well I heard the Olympia. Eddie Atkins was playing with the Olympia when he came back home. Edward Cleve, he came home several times.
Where was he from?
He was from St. James, but he had been down here.
What did Clem play like? What kind of style did Edward Cleve play?
He was a jazz trumpet player.
He wasn't a reading guy, huh?
No, he wasn't a reading guy, but he was a jazz player.
Do you remember any numbers that he featured or any kind of St. James Packer?
Mostly I heard him play with blues. He played the blues. If he liked that tiger, he'd see that up.
When was that that he played Tiger Rock?
Well that was long, about 28. Oh yeah.
I see. Let me think of some of the other old trumpet players. Who else did you hear, say around 1905? Do you remember any other trumpet players?
Not 1905, no. I hadn't started playing no music myself.
Well one time you mentioned Buddy Bolin to me. I just…

Buddy Bolin, I was quite young when he played. That might be around 1905 or 1906. But I heard him play it several times. He was a strong trumpet player. He was a strong trumpet player. He had that Jackson Street Hall, Long Termin Hall, and he hadn't played well at that Lincoln Park. You know he could blow.
Oh yeah. Well did you hear him here in the city or out in the country? Yeah. Oh you used to come in sometimes, huh?

Yeah I used to come here from… I've been coming here since 1902. I've been coming to the city. I've been seeing Mardi Gras since 1902. I've been coming up until during the war when they didn't have no war. I've been seeing every carnival that's been happening.
Well what was carnival like? Did they have much music there?

Well they didn't have as much music as they have today. Now it's a colored band from St. John Paris. I remember when they lead the Mardi Gras parade by the name of the Cuyall Pickwick. All red suit. There was a head band in the parade. It was a good band.
What kind of pickwick?
Cuyall Pickwick from St. John.
Cuyall?
Pickwick, yeah. Yeah. They lead the Mardi Gras parade.
What town in St. John would they be from?
They was from around Missouri. From St. John Paris.
I just wondered because I've heard Kit Thomas talk about him. You know Kit Thomas?
I know Kit Thomas but I never knew where Kit Thomas came from.
He's from Missouri. From Missouri? Edmund Hall is from up there too.
Yeah he's from up there too, yeah.
Yeah, all the Hall boys you know. They told me about that brass band up there. I think Kit Thomas' daddy played him.
That was the brass band. I heard him play it once or twice.
So you heard quite a bit of music at Mardi Gras then, huh? You had these brass bands.

Yes, yes. That's why I liked to hear the brass band on the Mardi Gras day. I've been hearing the band playing. I've been hearing the band playing. I've been hearing the band playing. Oh, they had more bands than they used to have. What else did they have besides brass bands at Mardi Gras?
Did you hear any orchestras or anything? Not doing like Mardi Gras day, no. They like the orchestra be playing now. They used to hear that. Well they have them on the trucks now.

Yeah. You see people you haven't seen for years on those trucks. All the time, yeah. But they didn't do that in those days. No, they didn't have no trucks. They were wagging. Did anybody follow the wrecks parade? Yeah, sure. Just like they do now.
Yeah, but I mean did they have wagons after the wrecks parade? Yeah, wagons.
Yeah, wagons.
Follow just like they followed with these trucks. Mm-hmm. But no one of them did.
You see people you haven't seen for years on those trucks. All the time, yeah.
But they didn't do that in those days.
No, they didn't have no trucks. No wagons.
Well, did anybody follow wrecks then?
Did anybody follow what?
Did anybody follow the wrecks parade?
Yeah, sure. Just like they do now.
Yeah, but I mean did they have wagons after the wrecks parade?
Yeah, wagons. Follow just like they follow with these trucks.
But no bands, huh?
Yeah, they always had bands, but not as many. Oh, I see.
But would they have bands on the wagons? Yeah.
Oh, I got it.
Yeah. I see what you mean.
You see like the, the, the, what's the name of them?
I just want to continue playing.
You still play today? I heard you play with the Eureka one time.
Let me play my song. Somebody stole my gap.
You were talking about the size of bands, and the orchestra wouldn't be big then.
No, it wasn't their biggest dance today.
How big would they get?
About six pieces.
Let's turn it off for a minute until you get straight.
You still play that old style. You didn't try to play modern or anything. Yeah, but it's the same old. Sounds good.
Yeah, that's what I like. Yeah, that's what I like. That's what I like. That's what I like. That's what I like. That's what I like.
That's what I like. That's what I like. That's what I like. That's what I like.
That's what I like.

That's what I like. That's what I like. That's what I like. That's what I like. That's what I like. That's what I like. That's what I like. That's what I like. That's what I like. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.
Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. That sounds good. That's nice. I was going to ask you, do you remember how Buddy Bolden played? No. Not clearly, huh? No. But do you remember Clem style? Can you play it again?
Clem play something in style that don't play any day.
Yeah. Mm-hmm. Play on that order, huh? Yeah. And who else do you remember that you could maybe give a little sample of that style? Is there anybody that you copied or anything?
I was trying to figure Luis, Luis, a good man, how he played. He played on the same style, though. Mm-hmm.
What about Chris Kelly?

Did you ever hear him? Chris Kelly, he was a jazz coach. Yeah, I heard him. He played on the style of Dixie Dan music. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. That's it. You ever heard this song, since Jesse said it to me, huh?
No, I don't believe it. You ever heard that?
Where'd you learn it?
I had a music, don't you? I got plenty of music. I just gotta study more. I done done them and I forgot them. Yeah, I have plenty of it.
I know how to grow the drummer along. Huh? I know how to grow the drummer along.
That might help you. Oh, yeah. Congratulations. That's great.
You got Advance in that march, huh? Yeah. Service by Harold Bennett. Published by Fillmore Music House Cincinnati. I would try to buy that book again,
but I couldn't get it.
Advance by Harold Bennett again. Fillmore Music House Cincinnati also. First clarinet poetry, huh? See that?

We had First, Solo, and Three. I had that one. I was playing the WPS band. Oh, you played with them too, huh? I had a play with them. This boy here, I had one of them learn how to play clarinet. He turned me to hurt his stomach. So, during the WPS time, he had a shovel and a wheelbar. I said, man, you've been playing in the band. You're not going to be a shoveling that wheelbar. This instrument was bought in 1929. It cost $178 in 1929. Well, that must be a fine home. Yeah, push it. It stood up all over the years.
